summary: Defines the properties of the QUIC transport protocol that hold for all versions of the protocol. These invariants are the parts that networks and endpoints can rely on staying the same as QUIC evolves.

plainLanguage.summary: QUIC is designed to be revised: two ends can agree to speak a newer version of it. This RFC writes down the small set of rules that no version is allowed to break, so that the network equipment sitting between the ends does not have to be updated every time QUIC changes.

questions: which parts of quic stay the same across versions
what is a quic connection id
how does quic version negotiation work
what is the difference between quic long and short headers
subtitle: The short list of QUIC properties that every version must keep, so new versions can always be deployed.

tldr.problem: QUIC is expected to change over time, with new versions negotiated between endpoints, but a protocol that can change anything is a protocol that can break. Networks in the path also tend to assume that what they see in one version means the same thing in the next.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists the properties that every version of QUIC must keep: the two header forms and how the first byte distinguishes them, the shape of the connection ID, the version field and its reserved value, and the version negotiation packet.
tldr.outcome: The result is that new QUIC versions can be deployed without breaking the parts of the protocol that intermediaries rely on. RFC 8999 is a Proposed Standard and was later updated by RFC 9368.

today: RFC 8999 is a Proposed Standard and was later updated by RFC 9368. It has not been obsoleted, so the invariants it lists are the ones every QUIC version still has to honour.

sections.title: An Abstract Description of QUIC
sections.content:
QUIC is a connection-oriented protocol between two endpoints. Those endpoints exchange UDP datagrams, and those datagrams contain QUIC packets. QUIC endpoints use QUIC packets to establish a QUIC connection, which is shared protocol state between those endpoints.

That is the whole description. Everything else in QUIC, from the encryption to the way streams are multiplexed, is a matter for the transport specification itself.
sections.plainLanguage: QUIC is a connection-oriented protocol carried inside UDP datagrams. Two ends use it to build a connection, which is the state they share while the conversation lasts.

sections.title: The Fixed Properties of Every Version
sections.content:
In addition to providing secure, multiplexed transport, QUIC allows for the option to negotiate a version. That is what lets the protocol change over time in response to new requirements, and many characteristics of the protocol could change between versions.

This document describes the subset of QUIC that is intended to remain stable as new versions are developed and deployed. All of these invariants are independent of the IP version. The primary goal is to ensure that it is possible to deploy new versions of QUIC: by documenting the properties that cannot change, the document aims to preserve the ability for QUIC endpoints to negotiate changes to any other aspect of the protocol. As a consequence it also guarantees a minimal amount of information that is made available to entities other than endpoints. Unless specifically prohibited, any aspect of the protocol can change between different versions.

The document defines requirements on future QUIC versions even where normative language is not used, and it uses terms and notational conventions from the QUIC transport specification. The packet formats are described with a notation in which complex fields are named and then followed by a list of fields, individual fields carry length information and indications about fixed value, optionality or repetition, and lengths are given in bits. The document uses network byte order, that is big endian values, and fields are placed starting from the high-order bits of each byte.
sections.plainLanguage: Only a few things are frozen. Everything else, including the encryption, may be different in the next version, as long as the two ends agree to use it.

sections.title: The Long Header
sections.content:
QUIC defines two types of packet headers, long and short. Packets with a long header are identified by the most significant bit of the first byte being set; packets with a short header have that bit cleared.

The long header carries a fixed set of fields. The first bit is the header form, fixed at 1, and the remaining seven bits of that byte are version specific. The next four bytes hold a 32-bit Version field. The next byte holds the length in bytes of the Destination Connection ID field that follows it, encoded as an 8-bit unsigned integer, and the Destination Connection ID field itself is between 0 and 255 bytes in length. The next byte likewise holds the length in bytes of the Source Connection ID field, encoded as an 8-bit unsigned integer, and that field is also between 0 and 255 bytes long. The remainder of the packet contains version-specific content.

Aside from the values described here, the payload of QUIC packets is version specific and of arbitrary length. A version of QUIC could permit multiple QUIC packets in a single UDP datagram, but the invariant properties only describe the first packet in a datagram.
sections.plainLanguage: The long header is used when the two ends need to agree on things, such as which version they are speaking. It carries the version number and the two identifiers that name the connection.

sections.title: The Short Header
sections.content:
A QUIC packet with a short header has the high bit of the first byte set to 0. It includes a Destination Connection ID immediately following the first byte, and its remaining seven bits are version specific. The short header does not include the Destination Connection ID Length, the Source Connection ID Length, the Source Connection ID, or the Version fields. The length of the Destination Connection ID is not encoded in packets with a short header and is not constrained by this specification. The remainder of the packet has version-specific semantics.

QUIC packets might be integrity protected, including the header. Version Negotiation packets are the exception, and are not integrity protected.
sections.plainLanguage: The short header is the compact one used once a connection is running. It carries only the identifier of the connection, so there is very little for the network to look at.

sections.title: The Connection ID
sections.content:
A connection ID is an opaque field of arbitrary length. Its primary function is to ensure that changes in addressing at lower protocol layers, in UDP and IP and below, do not cause packets for a QUIC connection to be delivered to the wrong QUIC endpoint. The connection ID is used by endpoints and the intermediaries that support them to ensure that each QUIC packet can be delivered to the correct instance of an endpoint. At the endpoint, it identifies the QUIC connection for which the packet is intended.

The connection ID is chosen by each endpoint using version-specific methods, and packets for the same QUIC connection might use different connection ID values.

The Version field contains a 4-byte identifier that can be used by endpoints to identify a QUIC version. A Version field with a value of 0x00000000 is reserved for version negotiation, and all other values are potentially valid. The properties described in the document apply to all versions of QUIC: a protocol that does not conform to them is not QUIC. Future documents might describe additional properties that apply to a specific version or to a range of versions.
sections.plainLanguage: The connection ID is a label the two ends agree on so that packets find their way even when the network rewrites addresses. The version number is a four-byte tag, and one value of it is reserved for saying "let us agree on a version".

sections.title: Version Negotiation
sections.content:
A QUIC endpoint that receives a packet with a long header and a version it either does not understand or does not support might send a Version Negotiation packet in response. Packets with a short header do not trigger version negotiation.

A Version Negotiation packet sets the high bit of the first byte, and thus conforms to the format of a long header packet. It is identifiable as such by its Version field, which is set to 0x00000000. Only the most significant bit of the first byte has any defined value; the remaining seven bits, labelled "Unused", can be set to any value when sending and MUST be ignored on receipt. After the Source Connection ID field, the packet contains a list of Supported Version fields, each identifying a version the sending endpoint supports, and no other fields. An endpoint MUST ignore a packet that contains no Supported Version fields, or that contains a truncated Supported Version value.

Version Negotiation packets do not use integrity or confidentiality protection. Specific QUIC versions might include protocol elements that allow endpoints to detect modification or corruption in the set of supported versions.

An endpoint MUST include the value from the Source Connection ID field of the packet it receives in the Destination Connection ID field, and the value for the Source Connection ID field MUST be copied from the Destination Connection ID field of the received packet, which is initially randomly selected by a client. Echoing both connection IDs gives clients some assurance that the server received the packet, and that the Version Negotiation packet was not generated by an attacker who is unable to observe packets. An endpoint that receives a Version Negotiation packet might change the version it decides to use for subsequent packets, and the conditions under which it does so depend on the version of QUIC it chooses.
sections.plainLanguage: When a server hears a version it does not know, it can send back a list of versions it does know. The reply is not protected in any way, so the client only trusts its contents after checking them itself.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
It is possible for middleboxes to observe traits of a specific version of QUIC and assume that when other versions exhibit similar traits the same underlying meaning is being expressed. There are potentially many such traits, and some effort has been made to either eliminate or obscure some observable traits in QUIC version 1, but many remain. Other QUIC versions might make different design decisions and so exhibit different traits.

The QUIC version number does not appear in all QUIC packets, which means that reliably extracting information from a flow based on version-specific traits requires that middleboxes retain state for every connection ID they see.

The Version Negotiation packet is not integrity protected and has only modest protection against insertion by attackers. An endpoint MUST authenticate the semantic content of a Version Negotiation packet if it attempts a different QUIC version as a result.
sections.plainLanguage: Equipment in the middle of the network can see the shape of what passes by it, and it may draw the wrong conclusion from what it sees in a later version. The version negotiation reply in particular can be forged, so a client must check it before acting on it.

sections.title: Assumptions That Are Not Safe
sections.content:
Appendix A lists a sampling of incorrect assumptions that might be made about QUIC based on knowledge of QUIC version 1. Some of these statements are not even true for QUIC version 1, and the list is not exhaustive. The document states that any and all of the following statements can be false for a given QUIC version.

Among them are that QUIC uses TLS and some TLS messages are visible on the wire; that QUIC long headers are only exchanged during connection establishment; that every flow on a given five-tuple will include a connection establishment phase; that the first packets exchanged on a flow use the long header; that the last packet before a long period of quiescence might be assumed to contain only an acknowledgment; that QUIC uses an AEAD_AES_128_GCM function to protect the packets it exchanges during connection establishment; that QUIC packet numbers are encrypted and appear as the first encrypted bytes; that QUIC packet numbers increase by one for every packet sent; that QUIC has a minimum size for the first handshake packet sent by a client; that QUIC stipulates that a client speak first; that QUIC packets always have the second bit of the first byte, 0x40, set; that a QUIC Version Negotiation packet is only sent by a server; that a QUIC connection ID changes infrequently; that QUIC endpoints change the version they speak if they are sent a Version Negotiation packet; that the Version field in a QUIC long header is the same in both directions; that a QUIC packet with a particular value in the Version field means that the corresponding version of QUIC is in use; and that only one connection at a time is established between any pair of QUIC endpoints.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC ends with a list of things people often assume about QUIC because of version 1, and warns that none of them is guaranteed. A future version may look quite different on the wire.

viz.caption: THE PROPERTIES THAT NEVER CHANGE BETWEEN QUIC VERSIONS

items.title: Two header forms
items.text: Long and short, told apart by the top bit of the first byte.

items.title: Connection ID
items.text: An opaque field of arbitrary length, chosen by each endpoint.

items.title: Version field
items.text: A 4-byte identifier; zero is reserved for version negotiation.

items.title: Integrity protection
items.text: Every QUIC packet is protected, except Version Negotiation packets.

data.code:
Long Header Packet {
  Header Form (1) = 1,
  Version-Specific Bits (7),
  Version (32),
  Destination Connection ID Length (8),
  Destination Connection ID (0..2040),
  Source Connection ID Length (8),
  Source Connection ID (0..2040),
  Version-Specific Data (..),
}

data.title: Version Negotiation Packet
data.code:
Version Negotiation Packet {
  Header Form (1) = 1,
  Unused (7),
  Version (32) = 0,
  Destination Connection ID Length (8),
  Destination Connection ID (0..2040),
  Source Connection ID Length (8),
  Source Connection ID (0..2040),
  Supported Version (32) ...,
}
